summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: In re Texas Department of Family & Protective Services
key_cases.holding: The mass removal of children from the YFZ Ranch was not warranted on the evidence, because Chapter 262 requires danger to the individual child and the Family Code gives courts ample authority to protect children without separating them from their parents.
key_cases.relevance: The Texas Supreme Court's controlling application of Family Code §§ 262.101-.201 at this node: danger must be proved as to the particular child, and the court must use the Code's lesser alternatives — orders restraining a party, removing the alleged perpetrator, or assisting the investigation — before separating a family.
key_cases.quote: the Family Code gives the district court broad authority to protect children short of separating them from their parents and placing them in foster care

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Fabricating evidence of child sexual abuse that causes a child's removal violates the parents' substantive due process right to family integrity and shocks the conscience.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the conscience-shocking standard that separates a mistaken emergency removal from an unconstitutional one.
key_cases.quote: the district court was correct in holding that a teacher's fabrication of sexual abuse against a student's father shocks the contemporary conscience

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Texas child-protection caseworkers who remove children are entitled to qualified, not absolute, immunity; on these facts the workers' temporary warrantless removal was objectively reasonable and violated no clearly established right, so qualified immunity applied.
key_cases.relevance: The foundational Fifth Circuit decision on what a Texas caseworker faces when she removes without a court order — qualified immunity measured by objective reasonableness against clearly established law at the time.
key_cases.quote: In these circumstances, we think that appellants’ actions in temporarily removing the children from the home were objectively reasonable, and as a matter of law violated no clearly established right.

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The government may not seize a child from his parents absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, exigency meaning reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely suffice. Because that law was not clearly established when these events occurred, every individual defendant received qualified immunity and summary judgment was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Fifth Circuit standard for a warrantless emergency removal in Texas, announced prospectively here after the panel granted immunity for past conduct.
key_cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: In writing before the department conducts an interview with an alleged perpetrator; the person signs the written notice to acknowledge receipt (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))
content_required: That the person may request an administrative review of the department's findings under Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309 (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))

Administrative review of a disputed determination of whether child abuse or neglect occurred is conducted by a department employee in administration who was not involved in and did not directly supervise the investigation, and the review must sustain, alter, or reverse the department's original findings (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(c))

The review must be conducted as soon as possible but not later than the 45th day after the date the department receives the request, unless the department has good cause for extending the deadline or a related court proceeding or criminal investigation is pending (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(d))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091; the department must document in the case file that it provided the notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(b)). A person is not required to exhaust the review remedy before pursuing a judicial remedy provided by law (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(e)), and when a finding is overturned the department must remove the person's name from the central registry not later than the 10th business day after it receives notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.002(b)(3))
